one_liner: Coq-proved generator of finite-field arithmetic in C, Rust, Go and Zig; matches hand-written Curve25519 field code in BoringSSL, not faster.
what_it_does: Fiat Cryptography is a Coq development whose extracted compiler (fiat_crypto) takes a prime and a word size and emits straight-line field arithmetic (carry_mul, carry_square, add, sub, opp, selectznz, to_bytes, from_bytes and more) for strategies such as unsaturated-solinas (Curve25519 5x51 or 10x25.5 limbs), word-by-word-montgomery (P-256, secp256k1) and dettman-multiplication. Pre-generated files ship in fiat-c/src, fiat-rust (the fiat-crypto crate), fiat-go, fiat-zig and fiat-bedrock2. It supplies only the field layer: the host library still writes the scalar-multiplication ladder, precomputed tables and protocol code, so it is not a drop-in for an X25519 or ECDSA API.
how_it_is_fast: It does not use a new algorithm; speed comes from emitting the same limb-scheduled, fully unrolled, branch-free multiply-and-reduce code an expert would write by hand (unsaturated Solinas reduction for 2^255-19, Montgomery word-by-word reduction for generic primes), with proven bounds that let it drop unnecessary carries. A value barrier (empty asm) keeps compilers from turning selectznz back into branches. Since 2023 BoringSSL also ships x86-64 ADX assembly that CryptOpt compiles from Fiat templates and checks with the translation validator in the Fiat repository.
when_to_use: You maintain a crypto library and want Curve25519, P-256, P-384, P-521, secp256k1 or Poly1305 field arithmetic with a machine-checked correctness proof at the speed of good hand-written C.
You need constant-time field code for an unusual prime (the generator covers 80+ primes and arbitrary Solinas or Montgomery-friendly moduli) rather than writing and auditing your own.
Portable 32-bit targets: the 10-limb 32-bit Curve25519 code is what the Linux kernel's generic 32-bit Curve25519 uses.
Rust projects that already depend on it indirectly (curve25519-dalek tests the fiat backend; the crate has about 151 million crates.io downloads) and want the formally verified backend selected.
when_not_to_use: You want a faster X25519 or Ed25519 than BoringSSL or OpenSSL: the only third-party runs show parity with BoringSSL's C and the old x86_64 assembly about 9% faster on arbitrary-point multiplication.
You need a complete protocol API (keygen, sign, verify, ECDH): Fiat stops at the field, so ladders, tables, encoding and side-channel hygiene of the rest are yours.
MSVC or other compilers without unsigned __int128 for the 64-bit unsaturated files; use the 32-bit variants there.
Regenerating code for new primes on a laptop: the toolchain needs Coq 9.0+ and OCaml 4.08+, a full build takes over an hour, and large primes can need a 1 GB stack and an hour per run.
The Java backend: the README marks it unmaintained and known buggy (issue #707).

integration.dependencies: none for the generated C (stdint.h only); generator needs Coq 9.0+ with Rocq stdlib 9.1+, OCaml 4.08+ and jq; Rust users take the fiat-crypto crate
integration.min_toolchain: C99-style C with GCC or clang for the 64-bit files (unsigned __int128 and __extension__); 32-bit files are plain C; Rust crate fiat-crypto 0.3.0 states no rust-version
integration.platforms: any two's-complement target (the files #error otherwise); 64-bit unsaturated code needs a compiler with 128-bit integers; the CryptOpt ADX assembly in BoringSSL is x86-64 with BMI2/ADX only
integration.thread_safety: Stateless pure functions on caller-provided limb arrays (no globals in fiat-c/src/curve25519_64.c), so safe to call concurrently on distinct outputs; not otherwise documented

gotchas: Proof scope: only the Bedrock2 backend has a proof that the emitted AST matches the internal semantics; the C, Rust, Go and Zig printers are unproven, the README says integer-size casts are not verified against what gcc or clang select, and it gives no quality guarantee for generated code.

Inputs must respect the typed bounds (loose versus tight field elements, e.g. call carry or carry_mul before feeding an add result to to_bytes); violating them voids the proofs and can overflow limbs silently.

The BoringSSL base-point speedup in commit 884086e (38817.1 versus 15095.3 ops/sec) comes from switching to the Ed25519 precomputed 30 kB table, not from faster field arithmetic; on arbitrary-point multiplication fiat64 was slower (13905.1 versus 15094.0 ops/sec).

Newer speed claims are for CryptOpt assembly, not the C: BoringSSL 43f8891 (2023, by fiat's lead author, reviewed by BoringSSL) reports +31.2% on Curve25519 arbitrary-point multiplication (28263.1 ops/sec) with no baseline row, CPU or compiler, and 20c9406 reports +63.5% P-256 ECDH on Cascade Lake but only under -DOPENSSL_SMALL=1 (against the small-footprint path, not nistz256), with no difference on Haswell.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Fiat when correctness proofs and coverage of many primes matter more than peak speed; ENG25519 (AVX-512 IFMA) and the amd64-64-24k Ed25519 code are faster on their target CPUs but carry no machine-checked proofs, and libsecp256k1 remains the complete, faster choice for secp256k1 signing rather than Fiat's bare secp256k1 field code.
verified_claims_summary: BoringSSL's bssl speed -filter 25519 runs show parity, not a speedup: in b2c312d (clang, 32-bit toolchain, Release, an unnamed Google Cloud Xeon with AVX2) the 32-bit fiat field code matched the previous C code on arbitrary-point and base-point multiplication and Ed25519 signing, with Ed25519 verify about 4% slower, and in 884086e (no CPU or compiler stated) fiat64 was about 9% slower than the old x86_64 assembly on arbitrary-point multiplication and won base-point multiplication only by using the Ed25519 table.
status_note: Actively maintained (Zig backend rewrite merged 2026-10-09) under a choice of MIT, Apache-2.0 or BSD-1-Clause; the generated C files are self-contained and easy to vendor, and BoringSSL, the Linux kernel's 32-bit Curve25519 and curve25519-dalek's fiat backend already do.
